tldr: Using the botched US Department of Justice releases as a case study, vonThenen demos how PDF, email and pixelation redactions get reversed, ending with his own blur-reading OCR model.
summary: David vonThenen, an AI/ML engineer presenting a personal side project, opened with the US Department of Justice document releases of December 2025 and January 2026. By his account, thousands of documents were pulled and re-uploaded within days because redactions failed, and he argued the effort went into shielding powerful people rather than victims. His first demo was the simplest failure: black boxes drawn over text that is still in the PDF, so copy-paste, or a script run across every file, reveals what was underneath.

He then walked through other loose threads. A PDF saved repeatedly but never flattened keeps its incremental updates, so a script can roll back to the oldest version. In a public puzzle PDF, he went into the object streams, took an ASCII85-encoded stream and decoded it to recover a removed passphrase. For email exhibits, the released pages included the raw MIME source, so OCR on the printed base64 attachment let him rebuild the original, unredacted image. He also sketched an idea he has not built: use named entity recognition on nearby, unredacted emails from the same time window and match candidate names against the width of each black box.

The image section covered open-source depixelation tools. A depixelation proof of concept recovered 'Hello from the other side' by matching block intensities against default OS fonts. UnPixel brute-forced fonts and sizes and identified the word 'admin' in Liberation Sans. DeepMosaics, a GAN-based restoration project, was used by someone to win a contest: a pixelated dialog in a video was moved around, so each frame gave another sample, and combining frames revealed the text.

His own approach skips image restoration entirely. Treat a redaction service as an oracle: feed it known text, collect the blurred or pixelated output, and train a narrow PyTorch OCR model (a connectionist temporal classification, or CTC, architecture) that maps damaged image to text. He compared this to model distillation by large AI companies. Training took about 14 hours on an H100, but the published safetensors model runs inference on a laptop CPU, and it read 'This is a test David' from a heavily blurred image. His conclusion: narrowing the problem to one obfuscation tool makes the attack feasible, and anyone else using that tool is then exposed.
keyPoints: Many released DOJ PDFs had black boxes drawn over live text; copy-paste or a text-extraction script recovered the hidden content across whole document sets.
PDFs saved incrementally without a final flatten keep earlier revisions, which a script can restore; individual object streams (e.g. ASCII85-encoded) can be decoded by hand.
Released emails included MIME metadata with base64-encoded attachments; OCR plus base64 decoding rebuilt the original, unredacted images.
Proposed but unbuilt attack: named entity recognition over surrounding emails from the same period, filtered by the pixel length of each black box, to guess redacted names.
Pixelation leaks information: depixelation tools match block intensities against rendered candidate text in known fonts and sizes (UnPixel found 'admin' in Liberation Sans).
Moving a pixelated region across video frames gives the attacker multiple samples; combined with DeepMosaics restoration, this recovered hidden file names.

vonThenen's CTC-based OCR model is trained on pairs generated by the target redaction tool and outputs text directly instead of restoring the image; training took about 14 hours on an H100, inference runs on CPU.
Narrowing the scope to one obfuscation service is what makes the attack feasible, and it then works against every other user of that service.
takeaways: Redact by deleting content, not by drawing shapes over it, and verify by extracting text from the exported PDF.
Flatten or re-export PDFs before publishing so incremental save history and leftover objects are gone.
Strip email headers, MIME parts and embedded attachments from anything you release, not just the visible body.
Never rely on blur or pixelation for text; replace sensitive text with solid fills, removing the original pixels, and do not reuse the same pixelation across video frames.
Treat any redaction or obfuscation service as attackable by someone who generates training data through it.

quotes.text: So not only can I just copy and paste, which is hysterical, but I can literally programmatically run across all documents.
In reality, a lot of hacking is pulling apart stupid mistakes or social engineering.

Trying to undo and unobfuscate the world is probably not a great idea, but if you reduce the scope of the problem to something that's far more doable, you probably have a much better chance at being successful.

chapters.title: Training a CTC model on redactions

watchIf: You publish redacted documents, screenshots or video, or build privacy tooling, and want to see the concrete ways visual hiding gets reversed.
